entities.name: Shwetaungtet
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Thiri Thihathura Shwetaungtet reigned as king of Sagaing from 1335/36 to 1339, a brief but tumultuous period marked by regicide and political instability in Upper Burma. His ascent to power was unconventional, achieved through the deposition of his own father, Tarabya, reflecting the volatile nature of royal succession in the post-Pinya era. Shwetaungtet's short rule is a significant episode in the early history of the Sagaing Kingdom, a state that emerged from the fragmentation of the former Myinsaing Kingdom following the collapse of the Pagan Empire.

Shwetaungtet seized the throne by orchestrating a coup against his father, King Tarabya, in 1335 or 1336. His reign, however, proved precarious and short-lived. Just three years into his kingship, in 1339, Shwetaungtet himself fell victim to the very forces of court intrigue he had leveraged. He was assassinated by loyalists of his deposed father, Tarabya, who sought to restore their former monarch or avenge his removal, plunging Sagaing into further dynastic chaos.

His assassination left the Sagaing throne vacant and ignited a fierce power struggle, eventually leading to the brief reign of Kyaswa, another son of Tarabya, who then sought to consolidate power and suppress the factions responsible for Shwetaungtet's demise. The violent end of Shwetaungtet underscored the fragility of political authority in the nascent Sagaing Kingdom and set a grim precedent for subsequent successions, contributing to a pattern of internecine conflict that characterized much of the kingdom's existence before its eventual absorption into the Ava Kingdom. The cycle of deposition and assassination during his time highlighted the fierce competition for power among the royal elite.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Shwetaungtet's brief but violent reign contributed to the chronic instability of the Sagaing Kingdom, setting a precedent for regicide and succession crises that weakened the state before its eventual absorption by Ava.
